promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The concept of a pure substance

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: In science, what does it mean to say a substance is 'pure'?
options: It is completely clean and safe to drink
It is made of only one type of particle (one element or one compound)
It comes from a natural source
questions.explain: In science a pure substance contains only one type of particle — a single element or a single compound. The everyday meanings ('clean', 'natural') are not the scientific definition.

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: Which of these is a pure substance?
questions.explain: Distilled water is only H₂O molecules, so it is pure. Sea water, air and a smoothie all contain more than one substance, so they are impure mixtures.

questions.q: What is a mixture?
options: Two or more substances that are chemically joined together
Two or more substances that are together but NOT chemically joined
A single element on its own
A liquid that has been boiled
questions.explain: In a mixture the substances are simply mixed, not chemically bonded, so they keep their own properties and can be separated again by physical methods.

questions.q: A cup of clear, colourless salty water looks just like plain water. Which statement is correct?
options: It is pure, because it looks clear
It is a mixture, because it contains water and dissolved salt
It is pure, because salt has disappeared
questions.explain: Looking clear does not make something pure. Salty water contains two substances (water and salt), so it is a mixture — the salt is dissolved, not gone.

questions.q: When a solid dissolves in a liquid, what do we call the solid that dissolves?
questions.explain: The solute is the thing that dissolves (e.g. salt). The solvent is the liquid it dissolves into (e.g. water), and the solution is the mixture you end up with.

questions.q: You stir sugar into water until it disappears. Which is the solvent?
questions.explain: The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving — here that is the water. The sugar is the solute and the sweet liquid is the solution.

questions.q: Which statement about dissolving is correct?
options: Dissolving is the same as melting
When a solid dissolves, its particles are destroyed
When a solid dissolves, its particles spread out through the liquid and are still there
Only hot liquids can act as solvents
questions.explain: Dissolving spreads the solute particles evenly through the solvent — they are too small to see but still present. It is not melting (which turns a solid into its own liquid) and no particles are destroyed.

questions.q: A substance that does NOT dissolve in a liquid is described as:
questions.explain: A solute that does not dissolve is insoluble (e.g. sand in water). One that does dissolve is soluble (e.g. salt in water).

questions.q: Which change usually lets MORE of a solid dissolve in water?
questions.explain: For most solids, a hotter solvent dissolves the solute faster and in larger amounts — which is why sugar dissolves more easily in hot tea than in cold water.

questions.q: Filtration is used to separate:
options: A dissolved solid from a solution
An insoluble solid from a liquid
questions.explain: Filtration traps an insoluble solid in the filter paper while the liquid passes through. It cannot separate a dissolved (soluble) solid, which slips through with the liquid.

questions.q: In filtration, what is the name for the liquid that passes through the filter paper?
questions.explain: The filtrate is the liquid that runs through the paper. The solid trapped in the paper is called the residue.

questions.q: Which mixture CANNOT be separated by filtration?
questions.explain: Salt is dissolved, so its tiny particles pass straight through the filter paper with the water. Sand, chalk and stones are insoluble, so they are trapped and can be filtered out.

questions.q: You want to get solid salt back from salty water. Which method should you use?
questions.explain: Evaporation gently heats the solution so the water turns to vapour and escapes, leaving the dissolved salt behind as crystals.

questions.q: A scientist wants to collect PURE WATER from salty water. Which technique keeps the water and leaves the salt behind?
questions.explain: Distillation boils off the water, then cools the vapour in a condenser back to pure liquid water, which is collected. The salt stays behind in the flask.

questions.q: In distillation apparatus, what is the job of the condenser?
options: To cool the vapour so it turns back into a liquid
questions.explain: The condenser is cooled (usually by cold water) so the vapour condenses back into a pure liquid that drips into the collecting container.

questions.q: Which task is chromatography best suited to?
options: Getting pure water from sea water
Finding out how many coloured dyes are in an ink
Removing salt crystals from a solution
questions.explain: Chromatography separates a mixture of coloured substances: each dye travels a different distance up the paper, so a single ink spot spreads into several separate spots.

questions.q: Why is the start line in paper chromatography drawn in pencil rather than pen?
options: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent, so it will not run and spoil the result
Pens are not allowed in labs
questions.explain: Pencil marks are graphite, which is insoluble in the solvent, so the start line stays put. Pen ink would dissolve and travel up the paper, ruining the chromatogram.

questions.q: How does the boiling point of a pure substance behave?
options: It boils over a wide range of temperatures
It boils at one exact, fixed temperature
It changes every time you test it
questions.explain: A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting and boiling point (pure water boils at 100 °C). A mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: Sample X boils sharply at 100 °C. Sample Y boils gradually from 101 °C to 106 °C. What does this tell you?
options: X is pure water; Y is a mixture (impure)
Y is pure; X is a mixture
questions.explain: A single sharp boiling point (X at 100 °C) shows a pure substance. Y boils over a range and above 100 °C, which shows it is impure — a mixture such as salty water.

questions.q: A mixture of sand and salty water is filtered, and the liquid that passes through is then evaporated. What is obtained?
options: Sand trapped in the filter paper, and salt crystals from the evaporating dish
questions.explain: Filtration traps the insoluble sand and lets the salty water through. Evaporating that filtrate drives off the water and leaves the dissolved salt as crystals, so both solids are recovered.
